title: Wash in the Jordan (2 Kings 5)
hook: a proud general wants a grand cure, and his servant girl's advice gets him healed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mantle, and a student who refused to leave his teacher. Your line was I will not leave you.

In the house of a great general, a young girl waits on his wife. She's from Israel, carried off in a raid. Her master is Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, and the King James Bible sums him up in one breath: "a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper." One day the girl says to her mistress: "Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy." A captive, wishing her captor well. He sets off with a letter from his king, and silver, gold and changes of clothing.

Naaman pulls up at Elisha's door with his chariot. Elisha doesn't even come out. He sends a messenger: "Go and wash in Jordan seven times, and thy flesh shall come again to thee, and thou shalt be clean." Naaman is furious, and the text lets us hear why: "Behold, I thought, He will surely come out to me, and stand, and call on the name of the LORD his God, and strike his hand over the place, and recover the leper." Instead: go take a bath, in a foreign river. "Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?" He turns and goes away in a rage. Then his servants come near with something wise: "My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?" So Naaman goes down and dips himself in the Jordan seven times, "and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean." Look who carries his healing to him. A captive girl. A messenger at the door. His own servants. Every step comes through someone with no rank at all. And the cure is plain water. The hard part was never the river. It was being willing to do something that small.
screen: `HEALED THROUGH THE ONES WITH NO RANK.`

segments.voice: Name the simple thing you've been putting off because it seems too small, or too ordinary for the size of your problem: making the doctor's appointment, saying sorry, answering the message you've left sitting, asking for help. If part of you says, like Naaman, behold, I thought it would be something bigger, let that go by, and picture yourself doing the plain thing, once. If you pray, you can bring it before God.
Naaman. A proud general who wanted a grand cure, nearly walked away, and was healed by washing in the Jordan, on the word of people with no rank.
Your line: just wash. Seven dips in a plain river, and a proud man made clean. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Naaman's washing in the Jordan as a picture of humility and of grace that can't be earned, and some churches connect it with baptism, which in the Gospels also happens in the Jordan.

what it means: a proud man wants a grand cure, and is healed by a plain one, on the advice of a captive girl and his own servants.
what a scholar hears: Naaman's 'behold, I thought' (5:11) is the knot; the servants' 'how much rather then' (5:13) unties it.

chat.says: Why was Naaman so angry when Elisha told him to just wash in the river?
options: He expected something grand; washing in a foreign river felt beneath him.
The Jordan was too cold that season, and he feared getting worse.
He thought Elisha was secretly trying to drown him in the deep river.
chat.meaning: Naaman wanted a grand cure, but his servants said: if he'd asked a great thing you'd do it; how much more, Wash, and be clean?

Samaria.meaning: the city where the prophet Elisha was

Abana and Pharpar.meaning: two rivers of Damascus that Naaman preferred

Elisha.meaning: the prophet who sent Naaman to wash

leper.meaning: in the King James, someone with a serious skin disease

notes: 'Leper/leprosy' is the KJV word; the Hebrew term covers a range of skin diseases. The script keeps the KJV word inside quotations only; a Keeper may want a gloss.
The index hook credits 'his servant girl's advice'; in the text the captive maid points him to the prophet (5:2–3) and his servants persuade him to wash (5:13). The script tells both.
The rest of 2 Kings 5 (Naaman's gift refused, the earth he takes home, Gehazi's greed) is not retold, to keep one idea.
howItsDone's baptism link (Jesus baptized in the Jordan, Mark 1:9) is attributed to 'some churches'.
